name: Na-makir / Namakir
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Sperlich, Wolfgang B. 1991. Namakir: a description of a central Vanuatu language. PhD thesis, University of Auckland (with 1993 revision supplement, vol. 2). ResearchSpace@Auckland,https://hdl.handle.net/2292/2314
catalog_quote: Stress in Na-makir is not phonemic. In general, stress falls on the penultimate syllable. A complication is the glottal stop, which appears to attract stress on to the following vowel, thus detracting from the general rule when such a glottal stop occurs in syllables other than the penultimate one. Common examples of penultimate stress assignment are (stress is indicated by the accent symbol ´): $ na $ bó $ kah $ 'pig' $ po $ po$ ká $ su $ 'jealous' $ na $ ta $ bé $ be $ 'butterfly' An example with a glottal stop attracting stress to the following vowel is na-boroboroʔak ('last words of a dying person') with the following syllable structure and stress placement: $ na $ bo $ ro $ bo $ roʔ $ ák $ i.e. the stress falls on the last syllable, or alternatively the stress is levelled over all syllables. Stress is also clearly reassigned in morphologically complex items (even if not always transparent in synchronic terms). For example the item $ bi $ ví $ la $ vil $ 'spotted, flecked' is complex and can be analysed ... as bi-vil-a-vil with vil being the base lexeme, bi- a formative, a insertion and reduplication. The stress in this case falls on the first $ vi $ or is level across all syllables. ... Similarly the nominalising suffix -ean carries stress (or at least levels the general stress rule), e.g. the morhologically complex na-dodo-ean 'love' yields: $ na $ do $ doéan $ ... where stress falls on the last syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and regularly penultimate (na-bókah, popokásu, natabébe). Two kinds of departure: a glottal stop pulls stress onto the vowel that follows it, which can yield final stress (na-boroboroʔák) or level stress across the word; and morphologically complex words may have stress reassigned (bi-víl-a-vil 'spotted', stress on first vi or level), with the nominalising suffix -ean carrying stress so that na-do-doéan 'love' is stressed on the last syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress; author mentions only the alternative of stress 'levelled over all syllables' in the exceptional cases.
new_statements.exceptions: (1) glottal stop attracts stress to the following vowel (final stress or level stress); (2) stress reassignment in morphologically complex items, e.g. bi-víl-a-vil; (3) nominaliser -ean carries stress ('or at least levels the general stress rule'), e.g. na-do-doéan with final stress. Elsewhere (2.2.2.3) a 'residual stress on the second vowel' of diphthongs in fast speech is mentioned.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for words in citation form, syllabified with $ boundaries; examples include the common article na- prefixed to nouns, i.e. the domain is the phonological word including the article. The 1993 revision supplement does not revise section 2.5 (errata for p. 80 only fix the spelling 'Na-makir').
new_statements.identity_note: Sperlich writes 'Namakir' (= Namakura, ISO nmk, nama1268; also 'Makura' in Ray 1926). His fieldwork was based mainly on Emae and Makira islands, i.e. the southern Makira-Emae-Mataso dialect area (he recognises only one dialect split, Tongoa-Tongariki-Buninga vs Makira-Emae-Mataso, thesis p. 15); no sub-glottocodes exist for these dialects. an earlier compilation had the right source but marked it unreachable; it is in fact open full-text on ResearchSpace@Auckland (hdl 2292/2314).

tone.quote: Among close relatives of Efatic, Lamen of Epi has regular penultimate (V2) stress (Early, 2002, p. 672). And Namakir, which has lost V1 as thoroughly as Nafsan has, presents today with stress on the final vowel, which is historically V2. This might lead one to suppose that Proto-Efatic also had V2 stress, and that the pattern in Nafsan is directly inherited from this. But Nguna presents a contrast.
tone.locator: p. 309, section 3.3.2 'Vowel loss and stress' (pp. 306-310), with Table 32 on the same page
tone.summary: No tone statement (silent); stress claimed to fall on the final vowel (historic V2 after loss of final vowels), e.g. ke-tamán, dualím - contra Sperlich 1991's penultimate rule.
